Cross-Validation & Information Criteria

Cross-cutting · the machinery for choosing a model and honestly estimating how good it is — the tuning engine behind every other page. Two routes to the same goal: information criteria (AIC/BIC) score complexity-vs-fit from a single fit, no hold-out needed; cross-validation re-uses the data as its own validation set. Used to set Ridge/Lasso alpha, tree depth on Decision Trees, k for clustering — and to keep bias and variance in balance.

Notation on this page. k is overloaded in the course (Lecture 5 uses it for both the number of parameters in AIC/BIC and the number of folds in CV). To stay unambiguous we follow the notation table: d = number of parameters (AIC/BIC), V = number of folds (CV), n = sample size, and the likelihood is written 𝓛 (“the slide writes L”). Where we quote a course formula verbatim we keep its symbols and note the mapping.

1. Essence

Two questions sit underneath every modelling task, and Lecture 5 (slide 3/11) insists they are different. Model selection asks “which model — or which hyperparameter — is best?”; its job is to pick the structure, and its tools are validation sets and information criteria. Model evaluation asks “how well will the chosen model do on data it has never seen?”; its job is to estimate real-world error honestly, and its tool is a held-out test set. The cardinal sin — repeated as the lecture’s first takeaway (slide 11/11) — is to tune on the test set: once you have used data to choose, that data can no longer give you an unbiased estimate of performance.

Information criteria (AIC, BIC) attack selection from one fit. They take the model’s likelihood — how well it explains the data — and penalize it for the number of parameters, so a more complex model only “wins” if its better fit outweighs its extra cost. The headline property: they need no hold-out set, just a likelihood, so they are fast and use all the data (Lecture 5, slide 6/11; slide 11/11).

Cross-validation attacks both selection and evaluation by recycling the data: split it into V folds, train on V−1, score on the one left out, rotate, and average. It assumes nothing about the model — no likelihood required — which is why Lecture 5 calls (stratified) CV “the gold standard” (slide 11/11). The cost is V model fits instead of one. Everything else on this page is a variation on these two ideas, and both are in service of the bias–variance trade-off: selection is the act of finding the complexity sweet spot.

2. When to use / when not to use

Reach for information criteria (AIC/BIC) when…

  • You have a model with a likelihood (OLS / logistic regression, Lasso paths) and want to compare nested or competing models cheaply — one fit, no hold-out (Lecture 5, slide 6/11).
  • Data is scarce and you can’t afford to carve off a validation set.
  • You want a parsimony bias: use BIC when you specifically want the simplest defensible model — its ln(n)·d penalty is heavier than AIC’s 2d, so it favours fewer parameters as n grows (slide 6/11).
  • You want to estimate out-of-sample error without a hold-out: that is exactly what AIC approximates (slide 6/11).

Reach for cross-validation when…

  • The model has no clean likelihood (kNN, trees, random forests, SVMs) — CV is model-agnostic and the course’s default tuning tool.
  • You are selecting a hyperparameter (alpha, k, max_depth) — score each candidate by CV and pick the best (§4).
  • You need an honest performance estimate and can spare the compute — CV is the gold standard (slide 11/11).
  • Classes are imbalanced → use stratified V-fold so every fold keeps the class ratio (slide 9/11).
  • n is small → LOOCV (V = n) is nearly unbiased (slide 9/11).

Watch out when…

  • Comparing AIC/BIC across different datasets or different targets → meaningless. The rule of thumb is lower is better, but only on the same data (Lecture 5, slide 6/11). An AIC of 4000 on one fit and 50 on another tells you nothing if they were not fit to the same y.
  • The model has no likelihood → AIC/BIC don’t apply; use CV.
  • LOOCV on a large n or a slow model → n refits is expensive (slide 9/11); prefer 5- or 10-fold.
  • You let the test set leak into selection → any preprocessing fit (scaling, feature selection) must live inside the CV loop / pipeline, or the estimate is optimistically biased. The course idiom wraps the scaler and estimator in make_pipeline precisely so the scaler is re-fit on each training fold (§3).
  • A single validation set drives many decisions → you can overfit that subset; CV (averaging over folds) is the antidote (slide 3/11).

3. Code idiom

The course teaches both routes with scikit-learn. There is no from-scratch implementation in the notebook — AIC/BIC are derived as markdown theory and the CV is delegated to sklearn estimators (notebook 08_Information_criteria_and_cross_validation (1).ipynb, cell 5).

Information criteria via the Lasso path (notebook 08_…, cell 6). LassoLarsIC fits the full Lasso regularization path and picks the alpha that minimizes the criterion. Note the make_pipeline wrapper so StandardScaler is re-fit per fit, and the set_params idiom for switching criterion:

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoLarsIC
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

# AIC: minimizes 2d − 2ln(𝓛) along the Lasso path
lasso_lars_ic = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LassoLarsIC(criterion="aic")).fit(X, y)
alpha_aic = lasso_lars_ic[-1].alpha_       # alpha that minimizes AIC
coefs     = lasso_lars_ic[-1].coef_        # coefficients at that alpha
zero_coefs = np.where(coefs == 0)[0]       # which features Lasso dropped

# Switch the same pipeline to BIC and refit (heavier penalty → simpler model)
lasso_lars_ic.set_params(lassolarsic__criterion="bic").fit(X, y)
alpha_bic = lasso_lars_ic[-1].alpha_

Cross-validated alpha (notebook 08_…, cells 11–12). Two solvers, two CV settings as written in the notebook:

from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV, LassoLarsCV

# coordinate descent, 10-fold CV
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LassoCV(cv=10)).fit(X, y)
lasso = model[-1]
lasso.alpha_       # CV-selected alpha
lasso.alphas_      # the alpha grid  ← attribute name
lasso.mse_path_    # MSE per (alpha, fold)

# least-angle regression, 20-fold CV
model2 = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LassoLarsCV(cv=20)).fit(X, y)
lasso2 = model2[-1]
lasso2.cv_alphas_  # the alpha grid  ← DIFFERENT attribute name

Real API difference worth memorizing. LassoCV exposes its grid as .alphas_ (cell 11) but LassoLarsCV exposes it as .cv_alphas_ (cell 12). Plotting the MSE path with the wrong attribute name raises AttributeError. This is a genuine sklearn distinction, not a typo. (Aside: the notebook uses cv=10 for LassoCV but cv=20 for LassoLarsCV, while a comment still says “10-fold” — a code/prose inconsistency, not an error; quote the actual cv=20 per the build rules. [VERIFY: intended cv=20 for Lars?])

Model-agnostic CV — the universal idiom (exercise 05_Model_selection_evaluation_and_assessment_VHL.ipynb, cells 2 & 5). cross_val_score for a quick estimate; GridSearchCV to search a hyperparameter grid:

from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, GridSearchCV

# one number per fold; .mean() summarizes, .std() is the CV variance
scores = cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k), X, y, cv=5)

# exhaustive grid search, scored by CV
param_grid = {"max_depth": [None, 2, 3, 4, 5],
              "min_samples_leaf": [1, 2, 3],
              "min_samples_split": [2, 3, 4]}
grid = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42), param_grid, cv=5, scoring="accuracy")
grid.fit(X, y)
grid.best_params_, grid.best_score_

4. Worked examples

Example 1 — do AIC, BIC and CV pick the same alpha? (diabetes + injected noise)

The notebook’s centrepiece is a stress test for feature selection (notebook 08_…, cells 2–3): take sklearn’s diabetes data (442 patients, 10 real features), scale it, then append 8 pure-noise features (random_00 … random_07, drawn with np.random.RandomState(10)). A good selector should keep the real signal and drop the noise. We then ask three selectors — AIC, BIC, and CV — for their alpha:

X, y = load_diabetes(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
X = X / X.std()
rng = np.random.RandomState(10)
X_random = pd.DataFrame(rng.randn(X.shape[0], 8),
                        columns=[f"random_{i:02d}" for i in range(8)])
X = pd.concat([X, X_random], axis=1)        # 442 × 18 (10 real + 8 noise)

Running the notebook’s exact code (computed, sklearn 1.8.0, the notebook stores no numeric outputs in our extract):

Selector chosen alpha # non-zero features (of 18) noise features kept
AIC (LassoLarsIC) ≈ 1.52 8 1 (random_07)
BIC (LassoLarsIC) ≈ 4.35 5 0
CV (LassoCV, cv=10) ≈ 1.70 8 1 (random_07)
CV (LassoLarsCV, cv=20) ≈ 1.39 9 2 (random_04, random_07)

(computed via ./.venv/Scripts/python.exe; the noise injection is seeded with RandomState(10), so these are reproducible.)

The story this tells: they do not all pick the same alpha, and the differences are exactly what the theory predicts. BIC’s heavier ln(n)·d penalty (with n = 442, ln 442 ≈ 6.1 vs AIC’s 2) forces the largest alpha, keeps the fewest features (5), and is the only selector that drops all the noise — a vivid demonstration that BIC favours simpler models (Lecture 5, slide 6/11). AIC and LassoCV land close to each other (~1.5–1.7) and each let one noise feature (random_07) slip through; LassoLarsCV’s lighter alpha keeps two. The lesson is the connective tissue of this whole site: the selection rule you choose changes the model you ship, and BIC↔︎AIC↔︎CV trade between parsimony and fit.

This is the same alpha that Ridge/Lasso need set, and the exam’s Assignment 1 sets it by CV on Hitters.csv. The general pattern — fit a path, score each alpha, pick the best — is what CV does for max_depth on a tree and k on a clusterer. CV is the tuning engine behind every method page.

Example 2 — choosing k for kNN by cross_val_score (Iris)

The model-agnostic route, straight from the course exercise (exercise 05_…_VHL.ipynb, cell 2). Loop k over a range, score each with 5-fold CV, plot the curve, read off the peak:

for k in range(1, 15):
    scores = cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k), X, y, cv=5)
    print(f"k={k}: CV accuracy = {scores.mean():.3f}")

Computed (sklearn 1.8.0, Iris is deterministic so no seed needed): accuracy rises then plateaus — k=1 gives 0.960, climbing to a 0.980 peak at k=7 and k=10, then easing back to 0.967 by k=15. (Searching k = 1…14 as the exercise does, the best is k=6 at 0.980.) Small k is high-variance (jagged boundary, sensitive to single points); large k is high-bias (over-smoothed) — the curve is the bias–variance trade-off made visible, and CV is what lets you see it without touching the test set. The per-fold spread (e.g. k=7: folds [0.967, 1.0, 0.967, 0.967, 1.0], std ≈ 0.016) is the variance of the CV estimate itself — see Diagnostics.

For a grid of several hyperparameters at once, GridSearchCV does the same search exhaustively. On Iris with a decision tree (exercise 05_…, cell 5) it returns best_params_ = {'max_depth': 3, 'min_samples_leaf': 1, 'min_samples_split': 2} at a best CV accuracy of 0.973 (computed) — the CV-chosen tree complexity, exactly the move Assignment 3 makes on breast-cancer data.

5. Visualization

The figure below is the AIC/BIC route from Example 1: each criterion as a function of alpha, with the chosen (minimizing) alpha marked. It makes the selection mechanism visible — you literally see each curve bottom out at a different alpha, and you see BIC’s minimum sitting to the right of AIC’s (a larger alpha, a simpler model). The notebook draws this with results.plot() plus vlines at alpha_aic/alpha_bic (notebook 08_…, cell 8); here it is rebuilt as an Observable Plot with the computed minimizing-alpha values marked.

famCross = (getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--family-cross').trim() || "#3D405B")
icData = {
  // log-spaced alpha grid; two illustrative convex criterion curves whose minima
  // sit at the COMPUTED minimizing alphas (AIC≈1.52, BIC≈4.35). Shapes schematic.
  const alphas = d3.range(0, 60).map(i => Math.pow(10, -1 + (3*i/59)));  // 0.1 … 100
  const aicMin = 1.52, bicMin = 4.35;
  const curve = (a, amin, base, scale) => base + scale*Math.pow(Math.log(a/amin), 2);
  const rows = [];
  for (const a of alphas) {
    rows.push({alpha: a, criterion: curve(a, aicMin, 4030, 95), kind: "AIC"});
    rows.push({alpha: a, criterion: curve(a, bicMin, 4075, 95), kind: "BIC"});
  }
  return rows;
}
Plot.plot({
  height: 320, marginLeft: 60, grid: true,
  x: {type: "log", label: "α (Lasso penalty, log scale)"},
  y: {label: "criterion (lower is better)", domain: [4000, 4600]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["AIC", "BIC"], range: [famCross, "#F18F01"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(icData, {x: "alpha", y: "criterion", stroke: "kind", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleX([1.52], {stroke: famCross, strokeDasharray: "4,3", strokeOpacity: 0.8}),
    Plot.ruleX([4.35], {stroke: "#F18F01", strokeDasharray: "4,3", strokeOpacity: 0.8}),
    Plot.text([{a: 1.52, l: "AIC α≈1.52"}], {x: "a", y: 4560, text: "l", fill: famCross, dx: -4, textAnchor: "end", fontSize: 11}),
    Plot.text([{a: 4.35, l: "BIC α≈4.35"}], {x: "a", y: 4560, text: "l", fill: "#F18F01", dx: 4, textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 11})
  ]
})

6. Diagnostics & interpretation

What to look at to decide whether your selection/evaluation is trustworthy:

  • AIC vs BIC divergence. When they pick the same model, you have a robust choice. When they disagree (as in Example 1: AIC keeps 8 features, BIC keeps 5), the gap is information — BIC’s ln(n)·d penalty is telling you the extra parameters AIC kept are weakly supported. Prefer BIC when parsimony matters, AIC when out-of-sample prediction is the goal (Lecture 5, slide 6/11). Report both; quote them only relative to each other on the same data.
  • CV variance (the fold spread). cross_val_score gives one number per fold; its standard deviation measures how stable the estimate is. A large spread means your performance estimate is itself uncertain — the cue to use more folds or repeated CV, which re-runs V-fold with fresh splits to reduce the variance of the estimate (slide 9/11).
  • The one-standard-error rule. When the CV curve is flat near its optimum, don’t blindly take the literal minimum. The 1-SE rule (Lecture 3, slide 19/20, for λ-selection) picks the simplest model within one standard error of the best CV score — a deliberate lean toward parsimony that guards against chasing noise in the CV estimate. This is the principled way to break a near-tie like Iris kNN’s k=6/7/10 plateau (§4).
  • Stratification check (classification). If classes are imbalanced, plain V-fold can produce folds with skewed (or missing) classes; stratified V-fold preserves the ratio and is “the gold standard” for classification (slide 9/11). sklearn uses stratified folds by default for classifiers in cross_val_score/GridSearchCV.
  • Did selection leak? Confirm scaling/feature-selection sit inside the pipeline (so they’re re-fit per fold) and that the test set was never touched during tuning (slide 3/11).

Comparative diagnostic: information criteria give you a number per model you can rank instantly (cheap, but needs a likelihood and assumes the model class is correctly specified); CV gives you a distribution of scores (richer — you see the variance — but costs V fits and any model). Match the tool to the question: AIC/BIC for fast likelihood-based comparison, CV for everything else.

7. Past-exam lens

How CV shows up. Cross-validation is the connective tissue of the entire Spring-2025 take-home: all four assignments tune hyperparameters via CV (phase0/exam_spring2025_notebook.md). Assignment 1 (Hitters.csv): use CV on the training set to find the optimal alpha for Ridge and Lasso, report the chosen values, then evaluate on the test set (item 1.6). Assignment 2 (WholesaleCustomers.csv): choose k for K-Means via the elbow method and/or silhouette score (item 2.4). Assignment 3 (wdbc.data): CV for tree complexity (item 3.3) and boosting parameters (item 3.5). Assignment 4 (SimulatedData.csv): general CV tuning with a hidden grader hold-out — the model must generalize (items 4.5, 4.8). The recurring workflow the grader expects is explicit: load → EDA → clean → encode/scale → split → model → tune via cross-validation → evaluate → compare → interpret. The grade rests on doing selection and evaluation separately — never tuning on the test set (Lecture 5, slide 3/11) — and on justifying the chosen hyperparameter, not just printing it. Information criteria do not appear as an exam task in 2025; they are lecture/notebook material (AIC/BIC on the diabetes example).

8. Math

Math is off. Use the Math toggle in the top bar to show the course-level derivation (and “full” for the rigorous version).

Mode A — course level. (Lecture 5, slide 6/11; notebook 08_…, cell 5.) The two information criteria score a model by its fit — the maximized likelihood \mathcal{L} — minus a penalty for its number of parameters d (n = sample size; the slide writes the likelihood L and uses k for the parameter count, which we relabel d per the notation table to free k for folds): \mathrm{AIC} = 2d - 2\ln(\mathcal{L}), \qquad \mathrm{BIC} = \ln(n)\,d - 2\ln(\mathcal{L}). Both share the same -2\ln(\mathcal{L}) fit term; they differ only in the per-parameter price — AIC charges 2, BIC charges \ln(n). Since \ln(n)>2 once n>e^{2}\approx 7.4 (computed), BIC’s penalty is heavier for any realistic sample, so it favours simpler models as n grows (slide 6/11) — exactly the divergence seen in Example 1, where with n=442, \ln(442)\approx 6.09 (computed) versus AIC’s 2. The slide’s rule of thumb: lower is better, and the values are comparable only on the same dataset. AIC estimates out-of-sample prediction error; neither needs a hold-out set, which is their headline advantage (slide 11/11).

Cross-validation (V-fold, slide 7/11) takes the opposite route — it estimates error directly by resampling, assuming no likelihood. The procedure: (1) shuffle the data; (2) split into V equal folds; (3) for each fold, hold it out as the test set, train on the other V−1, and score on the held-out fold; (4) summarize the V scores (their mean is the CV estimate, their spread its uncertainty). Three variants from slide 9/11: stratified V-fold preserves each fold’s class ratio (essential for imbalanced classes, “the gold standard”); leave-one-out (LOOCV) sets V = n so each fold is a single point — nearly unbiased but n refits expensive; repeated CV re-runs V-fold with fresh shuffles to reduce the variance of the estimate. CV serves the bias–variance trade-off; note the [R9-2] caveat that the course’s Total Error = Bias² + Variance (slide 10/11) omits the irreducible noise floor — the full decomposition is Err = σ² + Bias² + Var (ESL §7.3). See the math appendix.

Mode B — full rigor. (Anchored to ESL §7.5 (AIC), §7.7 (BIC) and §7.10 (cross-validation); ISL §6.1.3 (linear-model forms). Equation numbers are from the editions read.)

AIC — the optimism / Kullback–Leibler argument. Training error \overline{\mathrm{err}} is biased low as an estimate of in-sample error \mathrm{Err}_{\mathrm{in}}; the gap is the optimism \omega \equiv \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf y}(\mathrm{op}), and ESL shows that for many loss functions \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf y}(\mathrm{Err}_{\mathrm{in}}) = \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf y}(\overline{\mathrm{err}}) + \tfrac{2}{N}\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{Cov}(\hat y_i, y_i) \qquad \text{(ESL 7.22).} For a linear fit with d basis functions and additive-error variance \sigma_\varepsilon^2, \sum_i \mathrm{Cov}(\hat y_i, y_i) = d\,\sigma_\varepsilon^2 (ESL 7.23), so the expected optimism is exactly 2\,(d/N)\,\sigma_\varepsilon^2 (ESL 7.24). Adding this correction to \overline{\mathrm{err}} gives the C_p statistic C_p = \overline{\mathrm{err}} + 2\,(d/N)\,\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2 (ESL 7.26). The Akaike information criterion is the log-likelihood version, resting on the asymptotic (N\to\infty) relation -2\,\mathrm{E}[\log\mathrm{Pr}_{\hat\theta}(Y)] \approx -\tfrac{2}{N}\,\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{loglik}] + 2\,\tfrac{d}{N} \qquad \text{(ESL 7.27),} i.e. 2d/N is the asymptotic bias correction that turns maximized log-likelihood into an estimate of the expected KL-type prediction error. Hence \mathrm{AIC} = -\tfrac{2}{N}\,\mathrm{loglik} + 2\,\tfrac{d}{N} (ESL 7.29); minimizing this over a tuning parameter \alpha gives \mathrm{AIC}(\alpha) = \overline{\mathrm{err}}(\alpha) + 2\,\tfrac{d(\alpha)}{N}\,\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2 (ESL 7.30). Multiplying through by N recovers the course’s slide form 2d - 2\ln(\mathcal L).

BIC — the Laplace approximation to the marginal likelihood. ESL’s generic form \mathrm{BIC} = -2\cdot\mathrm{loglik} + (\log N)\,d (ESL 7.35) — the Schwarz criterion (times \tfrac12) — replaces AIC’s factor 2 with \log N; assuming N>e^{2}\approx 7.4 (computed) it penalizes complexity more heavily. Its derivation is Bayesian: with a prior \mathrm{Pr}(\theta_m\mid\mathcal M_m) the posterior model probability is \mathrm{Pr}(\mathcal M_m\mid\mathbf Z)\propto \mathrm{Pr}(\mathcal M_m)\int\mathrm{Pr}(\mathbf Z\mid\theta_m,\mathcal M_m)\,\mathrm{Pr}(\theta_m\mid\mathcal M_m)\,d\theta_m (ESL 7.37). A Laplace approximation of that integral about the MLE \hat\theta_m gives \log\mathrm{Pr}(\mathbf Z\mid\mathcal M_m) = \log\mathrm{Pr}(\mathbf Z\mid\hat\theta_m,\mathcal M_m) - \tfrac{d_m}{2}\log N + O(1) \qquad \text{(ESL 7.40),} where the -\tfrac{d_m}{2}\log N term comes from the determinant of the Hessian of the log-posterior at \hat\theta_m. Taking -2\log\mathrm{Pr}(\mathbf Z\mid\hat\theta_m,\mathcal M_m) as the loss reproduces BIC (7.35). Because BIC is asymptotically consistent (it selects the true model as N\to\infty) whereas AIC tends to over-select, the two answer different questions — recovery vs. prediction.

The ISL linear-model forms differ in scaling [R9-3]. For a least-squares fit with d predictors and noise estimate \hat\sigma^2, ISL writes C_p = \tfrac{1}{n}\!\left(\mathrm{RSS} + 2d\hat\sigma^2\right) (ISL 6.2), \mathrm{AIC} = \tfrac{1}{n}\!\left(\mathrm{RSS} + 2d\hat\sigma^2\right) (proportional to C_p, irrelevant constants dropped), and \mathrm{BIC} = \tfrac{1}{n}\!\left(\mathrm{RSS} + \log(n)\,d\hat\sigma^2\right) (ISL 6.3) — plus adjusted R^2 = 1 - \tfrac{\mathrm{RSS}/(n-d-1)}{\mathrm{TSS}/(n-1)} (ISL 6.4). These are unit-and-constant variants of the general likelihood forms — under a Gaussian model -2\,\mathrm{loglik} equals N\,\overline{\mathrm{err}}/\sigma_\varepsilon^2 up to a constant, the bridge ESL makes explicit in \mathrm{BIC} = \tfrac{N}{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}\!\left[\overline{\mathrm{err}} + (\log N)\tfrac{d}{N}\sigma_\varepsilon^2\right] (ESL 7.36) — so they select the same minimizing model in different units. (Note: the lecture cross-check [R9-3] and slide notes quote the AIC variant as \tfrac{1}{n\hat\sigma^2}(\mathrm{RSS}+2d\hat\sigma^2); the edition read here prints ISL 6.2 with prefactor \tfrac1n, not \tfrac{1}{n\hat\sigma^2} — the two differ by a further 1/\hat\sigma^2 scaling and still share the minimizer, but we report ISL’s printed \tfrac1n form.)

Cross-validation — equations and the bias–variance trade-off of the estimator. With \kappa:\{1,\dots,N\}\!\to\!\{1,\dots,K\} the fold-assignment and \hat f^{-\kappa(i)} the model fit with fold \kappa(i) removed, the CV estimate of prediction error is \mathrm{CV}(\hat f) = \tfrac{1}{N}\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{N} L\!\bigl(y_i,\,\hat f^{-\kappa(i)}(x_i)\bigr) \qquad \text{(ESL 7.48),} and over a tuning grid \mathrm{CV}(\hat f,\alpha) = \tfrac1N\sum_i L(y_i,\hat f^{-\kappa(i)}(x_i,\alpha)) (ESL 7.49), whose minimizer \hat\alpha is the selected model. The choice of K trades bias against variance in the estimator itself: K=N (LOOCV) is approximately unbiased for the true expected error but high-variance, because the N training sets are nearly identical and their errors highly correlated; small K lowers variance but, if the learning curve is still steep at the reduced training size, biases the estimate upward — so ESL recommends five- or ten-fold as a good compromise (Breiman & Spector 1992; Kohavi 1995). For linear smoothers \hat{\mathbf y}=\mathbf S\mathbf y, LOOCV has the closed form \mathrm{GCV}(\hat f)=\tfrac1N\sum_i\bigl[(y_i-\hat f(x_i))/(1-\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf S)/N)\bigr]^2 (ESL 7.52), and \mathrm{trace}(\mathbf S) is the effective number of parameters. When the CV curve is flat near its optimum, ESL/ISL apply the one-standard-error rule: choose the most parsimonious model whose CV error is within one standard error of the minimum (ESL §7.10, Fig. 7.9; ISL §6.1.3). Finally, CV must wrap the entire modelling pipeline — any supervised feature selection done before leaving folds out leaks the held-out samples and yields wildly optimistic error (ESL §7.10.2, “the wrong and right way”), which is the theoretical justification for the make_pipeline idiom in §3.
